body:
Understanding Gujarati literary forms

Gujarati literature has a rich tradition of narrative poetry, devotional songs, oral folk literature and modern poetic compositions. These literary forms differ in their purpose, subject matter, structure and relationship with music and social life.

Much of medieval Gujarati literature was composed in verse. Jain monks, Bhakti saints and narrative poets contributed significantly to its development. Their compositions preserved religious teachings, popular stories, cultural values and experiences of everyday life.

Rasa or Raso

Rasa, also called Raso, is an early Gujarati poetic form that developed into an important medium of narrative literature, particularly through the contributions of Jain poets.

Early Rasa compositions were associated with singing and rhythmic movement. Over time, the form developed into narrative poetry dealing with religious stories, biographies, historical events, heroic deeds and moral teachings.

Jain monks made extensive use of this literary form to communicate religious principles and narrate the lives of important personalities. However, not every Rasa composition dealt exclusively with religion.

Bharateshwar Bahubali Rasa

The most important early example is Bharateshwar Bahubali Rasa, composed by the Jain poet Shalibhadrasuri in 1185 CE.

The work narrates the conflict between Bharata and Bahubali, the sons of Rishabhadeva, the first Jain Tirthankara. It connects the pursuit of worldly power with the Jain ideal of renunciation.

It is recognised as the earliest available Gujarati literary composition bearing the designation Rasa. This does not mean that it is necessarily the earliest surviving composition in Gujarati literature.

Another notable example is Revantagiri Rasu by Vijayasenasuri, which describes the renovation of Jain temples on Girnar.

Distinguish literary Rasa or Raso from the folk dance called Raas and from the concept of rasa as an aesthetic emotion in Indian literary theory.

Akhyan

Akhyan is a narrative poem that presents a connected story through successive episodes, traditionally in a form suitable for oral narration and singing.

The subjects of Gujarati Akhyans were commonly drawn from the Ramayana, Mahabharata, Puranas and the lives of devotees. Poets adapted familiar stories into Gujarati, making them accessible to ordinary people.

Unlike a short devotional lyric expressing a particular feeling, an Akhyan develops a story through characters, events, dialogue and successive episodes.

Structure of an Akhyan

The characteristic structural unit of an Akhyan is called a Kadavu. In its mature form, a Kadavu generally consists of 3 parts:

  • Mukhbandh: The introductory portion indicating the episode that is about to be narrated.
  • Dhaal: The principal portion in which the episode is narrated in detail.
  • Valan or Uthalo: The concluding portion that closes the current episode and often introduces the next one.

This arrangement connects successive episodes into a continuous story. Early Akhyans did not necessarily contain all 3 components in their fully developed form.

Bhalan and Premanand

Bhalan, associated with Patan in Gujarat, is traditionally known as the father of Gujarati Akhyan. His important compositions include Dhruvakhyan, Mrugi Akhyan and Nalakhyan.

Premanand Bhatt, a prominent poet of the 17th century associated with Vadodara, brought the Akhyan form to maturity. His compositions are distinguished by effective narration, memorable characters and the expression of varied emotions.

Work by PremanandPrincipal subject
SudamacharitraKrishna and Sudama
NalakhyanNala and Damayanti
OkhaharanOkha and Aniruddha
MameruAn episode in the life of Narsinh Mehta
RanayajnaA narrative based on the Ramayana

Sudamacharitra is a representative example of Premanand's Akhyan poetry. It narrates the friendship between Krishna and Sudama and combines devotion with descriptions of human relationships and material hardship.

Bhalan and Premanand both composed works called Nalakhyan. Similarly, the story of Sudama appears in the compositions of Narsinh Mehta as well as Premanand. A familiar title does not always identify a unique author.

Prelims focus

  • Rasa or Raso was extensively developed by Jain poets.
  • Bharateshwar Bahubali Rasa: Shalibhadrasuri, 1185 CE.
  • Bhalan is traditionally called the father of Gujarati Akhyan.
  • Premanand brought Gujarati Akhyan to maturity.
  • Kadavu consists of Mukhbandh, Dhaal and Valan in its developed form.
  • Trap: Rasa as a literary form is not the same as Raas as a folk dance.

[References: GCERT, Class 7 Social Science, Gujarati medium, Chapter 8, Formation of Regional Culture, section on Gujarati language and literature; GCERT, Class 10 Social Science, Gujarati medium, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, p. 31; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Rasa/Raso, Bharateshwar Bahubali Rasa, Akhyan, Bhalan and Premanand; Gujarati Sahityakosh, Volume 3, entry Akhyan, Ekatra Foundation. Online references consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
The Bhakti tradition in Gujarati poetry

The Bhakti tradition encouraged poets to communicate religious devotion and spiritual ideas through compositions in regional languages. In Gujarat, short and singable poems became an important means of expressing devotion, moral teachings and philosophical understanding.

Narsinh Mehta, Mirabai and Dayaram are particularly important for understanding the Gujarati traditions of Pad, Prabhatiyu and Garbi.

Pad or Pada

A Pad is generally a short lyrical poem suited to singing, expressing a particular emotion, devotional experience, spiritual idea or message.

Pad occupied a central position in medieval Gujarati poetry. Its relatively compact form and accessible language allowed literary compositions to reach people through oral transmission.

Principal characteristics

  • It is generally lyrical and singable.
  • It often expresses a central emotion or spiritual idea.
  • It may contain a recurring line or refrain known as a Dhruvapankti or Tek.
  • Its subjects include devotion, divine love, spiritual knowledge, detachment and moral instruction.

Pad is a broad literary category. It is not restricted to Krishna devotion or to compositions intended for a particular time of day.

Narsinh Mehta

Narsinh Mehta was a 15th-century Gujarati saint-poet closely associated with Junagadh. He is traditionally honoured as the Adikavi of Gujarati literature.

His famous composition Vaishnav Jan To Tene Kahiye expresses the qualities of an ideal devotee, including compassion, humility and sensitivity towards the suffering of others. It is a well-known example of Gujarati devotional Pad.

Mirabai is also associated with devotional Pads expressing intense personal devotion to Krishna. Her compositions became popular in Gujarat as well as Rajasthan.

Prabhatiyu

A Prabhatiyu is a devotional song traditionally sung in the early morning. Its plural form is Prabhatiya.

The word is derived from Prabhat, meaning dawn. The morning provides a setting for remembering God, awakening spiritual awareness and reflecting upon the purpose of human life.

Some Prabhatiya describe the awakening of Krishna and the activities associated with the beginning of the day. Others communicate philosophical knowledge, devotion and the temporary nature of worldly existence.

Narsinh Mehta's Prabhatiya

Narsinh Mehta is the poet most prominently associated with this Gujarati literary tradition. A representative example is Jag Ne Jadava, in which Krishna is called upon to awaken.

Prabhatiya belong to the wider tradition of devotional Pads. A Pad may be sung at different times, whereas the designation Prabhatiyu specifically indicates its traditional association with the morning.

Garbi

Garbi is a Gujarati lyrical song associated with singing and dancing, particularly known in literary tradition for its expression of Krishna devotion and divine love.

Garbi developed within the broader tradition of Gujarati singable poetry. Its subject frequently involves Krishna, Radha and the Gopis, expressing affection, longing, separation and devotion.

Dayaram and Garbi

Dayaram, an important Gujarati poet of the late medieval Bhakti tradition, is especially celebrated for his Garbis.

He expressed devotion to Krishna through the emotions of the Gopis. This devotional attitude, in which the poet or speaker expresses love for Krishna from the perspective of a Gopi, is known as Gopibhava.

His well-known Garbis include:

  • Shyam Rang Samipe Na Javu
  • Vraj Vahalu Re Vaikunth Nahi Avu
  • Kaman Dise Chhe Alabela

These compositions express religious devotion through familiar human feelings and relationships. In Shyam Rang Samipe Na Javu, the speaker's apparent determination to avoid Krishna ultimately reveals her deep attachment to him.

Garbi and Garbo

Garbi and Garbo are closely related Gujarati song traditions, but their characteristic literary associations differ.

Garbi is particularly associated with Krishna devotion and the poetry of Dayaram. Garbo is commonly associated with the worship of the Mother Goddess and the Navratri tradition.

These are conventional associations rather than absolute restrictions on the subjects of every composition.

Prelims focus

  • Pad is a broad category of lyrical, singable poetry.
  • Vaishnav Jan To Tene Kahiye: Narsinh Mehta.
  • Prabhatiyu is traditionally sung at dawn.
  • Jag Ne Jadava: a Prabhatiyu associated with Narsinh Mehta.
  • Dayaram is especially associated with Garbi and Gopibhava.
  • Trap: Garbi is conventionally associated with Krishna devotion, while Garbo is commonly associated with Shakti worship.

[References: GCERT, Class 7 Social Science, Gujarati medium, Chapter 7, Bhakti Age: Religious Sects and Thinkers, sections on Narsinh Mehta and Mirabai; GCERT, Class 10 Social Science, Gujarati medium, Chapter 2, Cultural Heritage of India: Traditional Handicraft and Fine Arts, p. 15; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 8, Devotional Paths to the Divine, pp. 114–115; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Pad, Garbi-Garbo, Gujarat: Religion, Culture, Language and Literature, and Bargeet; Gujarati Sahityakosh, Volume 1, entry Garbi, Ekatra Foundation. Online references consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Oral folk literature in Gujarat

Gujarati folk literature preserves the experiences, emotions and customs of communities. Many folk songs are transmitted orally from one generation to another and exist in different regional versions.

Two distinctive song traditions are Fatana and Marasiya. They are associated with contrasting occasions and emotions: the humour of wedding celebrations and the sorrow of bereavement.

Fatana

Fatana are traditional humorous or teasing folk songs sung during Gujarati weddings.

Fatana belong to the broader category of Lagna Geet, meaning wedding songs. They are distinguished by their use of playful criticism, satire, jokes and sometimes exaggerated insults.

During a wedding, members of the bride's or groom's family may humorously tease the opposite family through songs. This creates amusement and reduces the formality of the occasion.

Characteristic features

  • Occasion: Marriage ceremonies and associated celebrations.
  • Dominant mood: Humour, amusement and playful teasing.
  • Subject: The bridegroom, wedding guests, relatives or members of the opposite family.
  • Tradition: Primarily oral folk literature, with considerable variation between communities.

Traditional songs may range from gentle teasing to considerably sharper mockery. Their defining characteristic is their humorous or satirical wedding context, rather than the use of uniformly polite language.

Representative example

Gharma Noti Khand is a traditional Fatana that humorously questions the wedding host's preparations. Like many wedding folk songs, it circulates in different versions rather than being identified with a single established literary author.

Jhaverchand Meghani collected Gujarati wedding songs in Chundadi: Gurjar Lagnageeto. His work is important for the preservation of oral wedding literature. He was a collector and editor of traditional songs, not necessarily their original composer.

Every Fatana is a type of wedding song, but not every wedding song is a Fatana. The distinguishing feature is humorous or mocking expression.

Marasiya

Marasiya are elegiac compositions that express sorrow over death, loss or a tragic event, often remembering the virtues of the deceased.

Marasiya are also known through Gujarati forms such as Marashiya and Marashiyu. They correspond broadly to the literary tradition of the elegy or lament.

In Gujarati folk culture, mourning songs give expression to grief, remembrance and separation. Some compositions praise the courage, generosity, character or achievements of the deceased.

The term is not limited to songs sung at funerals. Literary Marasiya may also commemorate a deceased person or a tragic event outside an immediate mourning ceremony.

Representative Gujarati example

Satan-Visal Sambhare, preserved in Jhaverchand Meghani's Ritugeeto, is an example of the Gujarati Marasiya tradition. It expresses remembrance of the deceased Visal through descriptions of the changing seasons.

This example illustrates how the sorrow of separation can be expressed through natural surroundings and memories rather than through a simple account of death.

In the wider Indian literary tradition, Marasiya are particularly associated with mourning the martyrdom of Imam Husain at Karbala. Gujarati mourning poetry, however, is not restricted to that religious context.

Distinguishing Fatana from Marasiya

FeatureFatanaMarasiya
Typical occasionWeddingDeath or bereavement
Dominant emotionHumourGrief
PurposePlayful teasingMourning and remembrance
English descriptionHumorous wedding songElegy or lament
ExampleGharma Noti KhandSatan-Visal Sambhare

Prelims focus

  • Fatana are humorous or teasing Gujarati wedding songs.
  • Fatana are a specific category within Lagna Geet.
  • Marasiya express grief, mourning or remembrance.
  • Chundadi is Jhaverchand Meghani's collection of Gujarati wedding songs.
  • Satan-Visal Sambhare is an example of Marasiya preserved in Ritugeeto.
  • Trap: Marasiya are not wedding songs, and the term is not restricted exclusively to religious mourning associated with Karbala.

[References: Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries Fatana, Marasiya and Meghani, Jhaverchand Kalidas; Jhaverchand Meghani, Ritugeeto, section Mitravirahana Marashiya, composition Satan-Visal Sambhare, available through Gujarati Wikisource; Amarkathao, Gujarati Lagna Geet Fatana Collection, entry Gharma Noti Khand. Online references consulted 26 November 2026.]
